body:
What cyber warfare concerns

Cyber warfare refers to cyber operations associated with military or strategic conflict that affect computer systems, networks, software or digital information. Such operations may seek to obtain information, alter data, interrupt services or undermine the functioning of connected systems.

Modern defence equipment frequently contains computers. A radar station, navigation facility or communication centre may use software to process signals, store information and distribute the resulting data. Consequently, the same military activity can depend on both the electromagnetic spectrum and a digital network.

However, electronic warfare and cyber warfare are not identical. Electronic warfare principally concerns military use and control of electromagnetic energy. Cyber operations principally concern digital information systems and their functioning. Their effects can overlap when radio-dependent equipment is connected to computers and networks.

The 3 central goals of information security

Cybersecurity is often explained through the confidentiality, integrity and availability principles, commonly called the CIA triad.

PrincipleMeaningDefence example
ConfidentialityInformation is available only to authorised parties.Preventing unauthorised reading of a protected message.
IntegrityInformation remains accurate and is protected from unauthorised alteration.Detecting an improperly changed position report.
AvailabilityAuthorised users can obtain information and services when needed.Keeping a command network usable during disruption.

A system can satisfy one goal while failing another. For instance, an encrypted message may remain confidential, but a communication outage may prevent its timely delivery. A computer system may remain accessible while containing inaccurate information. Therefore, the 3 principles must be considered separately.

Common forms of cyber threats

At the introductory level, cyber threats can be understood by examining what happens to information or a service:

  • Unauthorised access: A person or program gains access to information or resources without permission.
  • Data theft: Protected information is copied or disclosed to an unauthorised party.
  • Data manipulation: Stored or transmitted information is changed improperly, affecting integrity.
  • Malicious software: Software is used to damage, manipulate or interfere with systems.
  • Service disruption: Legitimate users are prevented from accessing an essential digital service.

Not every cybersecurity incident is an act of warfare. The term cyber warfare involves a military or strategic conflict context; accidental software failures and ordinary cybercrime are not automatically warfare.

Where cyber and electronic threats meet

Consider a satellite-supported communication system consisting of a radio terminal, a satellite link, a ground station and computers that process received information.

  • If unwanted electromagnetic energy prevents a terminal from receiving a radio signal, the immediate problem concerns the electromagnetic link.
  • If an unauthorised actor changes information in the ground station's computer system, the immediate problem concerns digital integrity.
  • If misleading radio-navigation signals cause a receiver to calculate an incorrect position, the immediate problem may involve electromagnetic deception, even without unauthorised access to its software.
  • If a computer's stored position data is modified without permission, the problem concerns cybersecurity, even if radio reception remains normal.

A wrong position report therefore does not automatically establish the cause. It may result from sensor error, radio interference, deceptive signals, software malfunction or improper data alteration. Identifying the affected part of the system is essential for distinguishing the concepts.

Protecting an integrated defence network

An integrated system needs protection at several levels. Reliable communication links help information travel. Authentication and integrity checks help establish whether received information should be trusted. Access controls and system monitoring help protect computers. Alternative communication and processing arrangements support continued operation when one component becomes unavailable.

India has a Defence Cyber Agency under the Ministry of Defence. In a statement dated 4 August 2021, the Ministry of Defence reported that the agency was fully functional and that the Army, Navy and Air Force had established their respective Cyber Emergency Response Teams.

These institutional measures address cyber threats. They should not be confused with a satellite programme or an electronic-warfare receiver.

Prelims focus

  • Confidentiality concerns unauthorised disclosure; integrity concerns improper alteration.
  • Availability concerns timely access to information and services.
  • Electronic warfare focuses on electromagnetic activity; cyber warfare focuses on digital systems in a strategic or military context.
  • Radio-navigation deception need not involve a software intrusion.
  • The Ministry of Defence confirmed the Defence Cyber Agency was functional on 4 August 2021.
  • Trap: An incorrect digital position report does not, by itself, prove that the receiver was electronically jammed.

[Sources: National Institute of Standards and Technology, Information Security glossary and Special Publication 1800-26, Executive Summary, consulted 14 November 2026; DRDO/DESIDOC, Electronic Warfare, 1988, Chapter 2, Electronic Warfare Definitions; International Telecommunication Union, Preventing Harmful Radio Interference, Overview, consulted 14 November 2026; Ministry of Defence, Press Information Bureau, Cyber Warfare, 4 August 2021.]

title: Cyber Warfare and Its Intersection with Electronic Warfare

body:
What a satellite is

A satellite is an object that revolves around another body under the influence of gravity. The Moon is a natural satellite of Earth. An artificial satellite is a human-made object placed in orbit for a particular purpose, such as communication, navigation, Earth observation or scientific measurement.

A satellite mission generally involves more than the object in orbit. Its essential elements include:

  • Space segment: The satellite or group of satellites carrying the equipment needed for the mission.
  • Ground segment: Stations and control facilities that operate the satellite, receive information or provide necessary support.
  • User segment: The equipment and people that use the service, such as navigation receivers, communication terminals or image-analysis centres.

A launch vehicle carries a satellite towards space. A launch vehicle and a satellite are not the same thing. The satellite's payload is the mission-specific equipment, such as a communication transponder, imaging instrument or navigation-signal generator.

Why orbital choice matters

An orbit influences how far a satellite is from Earth, the area it can observe, how quickly it moves across the sky and how frequently it can provide a service to a particular place. No single orbit is ideal for every mission.

Low Earth orbit

Low Earth orbit (LEO) generally refers to orbital altitudes below about 2,000 km. A satellite in LEO is relatively close to Earth and moves rapidly around it. This makes LEO suitable for many Earth-observation tasks because proximity can support detailed observation.

However, a single LEO satellite normally passes over a particular region for a limited period and then moves away. Continuous coverage of the same region may require several satellites or a different orbital arrangement.

Medium Earth orbit

Medium Earth orbit (MEO) lies between LEO and the geostationary orbital region. It is used for several purposes, especially by many global satellite-navigation constellations.

It is important not to assume that every navigation satellite must be in MEO. India's NavIC system uses a design involving geostationary and inclined geosynchronous satellites.

Geosynchronous and geostationary orbits

A satellite in a geosynchronous orbit has an orbital period equal to Earth's rotation period relative to the stars. Such a satellite does not necessarily appear fixed at one point in the sky: its orbit may be inclined or elliptical.

A geostationary orbit (GEO) is a special kind of geosynchronous orbit. It is circular, lies directly above the equator and has the same direction of revolution as Earth's rotation. The satellite takes approximately 23 hours and 56 minutes to complete an orbit and appears nearly stationary to an observer on Earth.

The geostationary orbital altitude is approximately 35,786 km above Earth's surface. GEO is valuable for continuous coverage of broad regions, particularly for communication and weather observation. Its greater distance makes it less suitable than many lower orbits for obtaining highly detailed images of small surface features.

Polar and sun-synchronous orbits

A polar orbit passes over or near Earth's polar regions. As Earth rotates beneath the satellite, successive passes can cover different parts of the planet. This arrangement is useful for widespread Earth observation.

A sun-synchronous orbit (SSO) is a special type of near-polar orbit designed so that a satellite passes over a given region at approximately the same local solar time. Similar illumination conditions help compare observations collected on different dates.

LEO describes an altitude range, while polar and sun-synchronous describe particular orbital characteristics. Consequently, one satellite may be described as both a low-Earth-orbit satellite and a sun-synchronous satellite.

Transfer orbit is not necessarily the final orbit

A spacecraft intended for geostationary service may first be placed into a geostationary transfer orbit (GTO). GTO is generally an elliptical orbit used as an intermediate stage before the spacecraft reaches its intended operational orbit.

The spacecraft may need further orbital changes after launch. Therefore, successful launch and successful entry into an initial transfer orbit do not automatically establish that the satellite has reached its final operating position.

OrbitDefining characteristicCommon application
LEOUsually below 2,000 kmEarth observation
MEOBetween LEO and GEOMany navigation constellations
GEOEquatorial, circular, approximately 35,786 kmRegional communication
Polar or SSONear-polar path; SSO maintains similar local solar timeRepeated Earth observation

Prelims focus

  • LEO generally extends to altitudes below about 2,000 km.
  • GEO is approximately 35,786 km above Earth's surface.
  • A geostationary satellite appears fixed because its orbit matches Earth's rotation.
  • Every geostationary orbit is geosynchronous, but not every geosynchronous orbit is geostationary.
  • Sun-synchronous orbits support observations at similar local solar times.
  • Trap: Reaching GTO does not necessarily mean that a satellite has reached its final geostationary orbit.

[Sources: NCERT, The Earth: Our Habitat, Class 6, Chapter 1, The Earth in the Solar System, printed p. 5; European Space Agency, Types of Orbits, sections on Low Earth Orbit, Polar Orbit, Sun-Synchronous Orbit, Medium Earth Orbit, Geostationary Orbit and Geostationary Transfer Orbit, consulted 14 November 2026; European Space Agency, Spacecraft Orbits, Geostationary and Geosynchronous Orbits section, consulted 14 November 2026.]

title: Satellites, Ground Systems and Orbital Choices

body:
Space reconnaissance and surveillance

Reconnaissance is the collection of information about a location, object or activity. Surveillance involves observing a region or activity systematically, often over a period of time. Both may use satellites, aircraft, ground sensors and other information sources.

Satellite reconnaissance helps provide observations of large or inaccessible regions without requiring an observer to be physically present on the ground. Applications include monitoring terrain changes, maritime areas, infrastructure and other features of operational interest.

However, the ability to observe a broad area is not the same as continuous observation of every point within it. A satellite's orbit, sensor capability, weather and observation schedule all influence the information that can be collected.

Different sensors collect different information

Optical imaging

Optical sensors record reflected visible light and, in some systems, nearby portions of the spectrum. They can produce images showing surface features such as roads, coastlines, buildings and land-use patterns.

Ordinary passive visible-light imaging depends on illumination, mainly sunlight. Thick clouds can obstruct the view of the surface. Consequently, an optical satellite does not automatically provide clear images through cloud cover or in darkness.

Radar imaging

Radar imaging uses transmitted electromagnetic waves and their returns to obtain information about the surface. Because radar supplies its own transmitted energy, it is an active sensing method.

Synthetic aperture radar (SAR) is a radar-imaging technique that can collect useful observations during day or night and through many cloud conditions. This makes it valuable when ordinary optical observations are limited by darkness or cloud cover.

The phrase all-weather imaging should not be interpreted as a guarantee of perfect observations under every condition. Image quality and usefulness still depend on the sensor, surface and environmental conditions.

Infrared observation

Thermal infrared sensors measure emitted infrared radiation and can reveal temperature differences. They can operate without visible sunlight, but atmospheric conditions and temperature contrast affect what they can detect.

Infrared observation is particularly important in understanding some early-warning technologies because a missile launch can produce a strong thermal signature.

Electromagnetic-emission measurement

Some space instruments observe electromagnetic emissions from sources rather than forming ordinary pictures of the ground. The resulting measurements can provide information about spectrum activity.

Thus, a satellite designed to measure electromagnetic emissions should not automatically be classified as an optical-imaging or communication satellite.

Early-warning systems

Early warning means obtaining and communicating information about a developing threat sufficiently early to support a response. It describes the purpose of a system, not a particular orbit or type of vehicle.

Early-warning sensors may be located on the ground, aboard aircraft or in space.

  • Ground-based radar can detect and track objects within its effective coverage.
  • Airborne early-warning and control (AEW&C) aircraft carry sensors that observe surrounding airspace and relay information to other users.
  • Space-based infrared early-warning systems can detect thermal signatures associated with missile launches and pass information to warning and command systems.

India's NETRA system, developed through DRDO, is an example of an AEW&C system mounted on an aircraft. It is not a satellite. Its mission includes detecting airborne and sea-surface targets and providing warning information.

As an international example of the space-based category, the United States Space Force describes its Space Based Infrared System (SBIRS) as using infrared sensors for missile early warning. This illustrates how an orbiting sensor may support warning, but it does not establish that every infrared satellite is a missile-warning satellite.

Navigation is different from reconnaissance

Satellite navigation determines position and provides timing information using signals transmitted by navigation satellites. A receiver measures information from multiple suitable satellite signals and uses it to calculate its position and time.

This is fundamentally different from satellite imaging. A navigation receiver generally determines its own position from received signals; the satellites do not need to photograph the receiver or continuously transmit images of its surroundings.

Navigation information can support aircraft, ships, ground vehicles and emergency services. Accurate timing can also support the synchronisation of communication and other infrastructure networks.

GPS, operated by the United States, is a global satellite-navigation system. India's NavIC is designed primarily for regional positioning, navigation and timing services. The geographical coverage of a navigation system must not be confused with the location of the country that operates it.

Reconnaissance gathers information about places and activities. Early warning detects a developing threat. Navigation provides position and timing. A satellite or another platform may support one or more of these functions, but the functions are not interchangeable.

Prelims focus

  • Passive optical imaging depends on available light and is affected by cloud cover.
  • SAR is an active radar-imaging technique that can observe during day or night through many cloud conditions.
  • Thermal infrared sensing can support detection of missile-launch heat signatures.
  • NETRA is an aircraft-based AEW&C system developed through DRDO.
  • Satellite navigation provides position and timing information without requiring the satellite to photograph the user.
  • Trap: Early warning is a function; it is not necessarily performed by a satellite.

[Sources: NASA Earth Observatory, Tracking Amazon Deforestation from Above, section explaining synthetic aperture radar, consulted 14 November 2026; NASA Earthdata ARSET, An Introduction to Synthetic Aperture Radar and Its Applications, 2 October 2024; DRDO, NETRA, Product Description, consulted 14 November 2026; United States Space Force, Space Based Infrared System, Mission and System Features, consulted 14 November 2026; ISRO, Satellite Navigation Services, NavIC section, consulted 14 November 2026.]
